rationale: A single-operator extension of the archive's best signal, but the industry-demeaning of the own-norm capex deviation is economically motivated (idiosyncratic restraint vs. sector capex cycle) and directly targets the diagnosed FMB-strong/alpha-weak pattern, so it is a defensible if incremental test rather than a cosmetic rescaling.

The inventory-intensity leg edges toward the well-documented inventory-growth anomaly (Thomas–Zhang, Belo–Lin), but recasting it as an own-norm deviation interacted with a profit windfall is a legitimate and clearly stated test of whether the mechanism is capex-specific or general operating-asset restraint.

The two legs are mechanically linked — above-norm EBITDA largely produces above-norm cash balances — so the product is closer to a squared profitability-windfall signal than to a measure of a deliberate retention-versus-reinvestment policy, and the cash-holdings level effect (Palazzo 2012) is itself a known anomaly.

The hypothesis claims a screen ("requiring that revenue still be expanding") and the type is declared conditional, but SUMRANK implements a purely additive tilt in which a large profitability deviation can fully offset outright revenue contraction, so the expression does not do what the economics asks and also imports an uncontrolled sales-growth tilt.

A well-motivated repair of the archive's worst failure that replaces scale-driven headcount growth with own-norm labor intensity, though it partially overlaps with the profitability leg (falling employees per sales dollar mechanically accompanies margin expansion) and will read in part as a labor-productivity signal.

Both legs are driven by the same underlying fact of a stagnant capital base — a firm that stops investing automatically shows above-norm sales-to-gross-PPE and below-norm capex-to-net-PPE — so the "joint occurrence" claim is undermined by mechanical denominator overlap and the signal risks being a doubled low-investment bet rather than utilization × restraint.
